intro: Each suggestion is a decision waiting to be made, not a change that has been made. Read the trade-off, record a lean, and only then implement. The board stores your selection in this browser only (localStorage); it is not sent anywhere, and no suggestion is applied by this site.
decision_gate: Is the missing information identified on the card actually missing, or is it already answered on the Questions page?
Does the suggestion change what a reader would decide, or only how it looks?
What is the cost of being wrong (wrong data shown as verified, credential exposure, misleading P&L)?
Can it be verified from an official Kalshi source, and is that source linked?
Is it reversible in one commit?

items.title: Run demo trade execution from a GitHub Actions job, not the browser
items.problem: Trading needs a private key. A private key cannot live in a public static site, so today's public site can neither read the portfolio nor place orders.

options.label: Actions-based trader
options.detail: Store the demo key pair as encrypted repository secrets. A scheduled workflow (or a manual workflow_dispatch with typed parameters) signs orders server-side and commits fills and positions to data/. The site stays read-only and shows results on the next build.
options.risk: Automated orders still trade mock money; a bug in the strategy spends the demo balance. Secrets are protected by GitHub, not by the site.

options.label: Small authenticated backend
options.detail: A separate service (for example a Cloudflare Worker or a small VPS) holds the key, exposes only read endpoints plus an order endpoint protected by a login you control.
options.risk: New infrastructure to own and patch; still no real money, so the value may not justify the effort.

options.label: Keep trading out of scope
options.detail: Leave portfolio and trading disabled and say so plainly, as the site does now.
options.risk: The original brief asked for execution and performance tracking, so this leaves part of the brief unmet.

items.why: It is the smallest change that satisfies the brief without exposing a key: secrets stay in GitHub, the audit trail is the commit history, and the site remains static and safe. B is the right answer only if orders must be placed interactively within seconds.
unlocks: Strategy categories grounded in real fills

items.title: Fix the definition of 'highest dollar amount'
items.problem: Kalshi exposes volume in contracts, not dollars. Three different rankings are defensible and they disagree: lifetime notional (volume × last price), 24-hour notional, and open interest in dollars.

options.label: Default to open-interest dollars
options.detail: Ranks by the money currently at risk in the market rather than by turnover that may be years old.
options.risk: Quiet but large markets outrank busy ones.

options.label: Default to 24-hour notional
options.detail: Ranks by recent activity, which matches an intuitive reading of 'live events with the most money moving'.
options.risk: Volatile; a new market can top the list on a handful of trades.

options.label: Compute true dollar turnover from trades
options.detail: Aggregate count_fp × yes_price_dollars over /markets/trades for the in-scope tickers.
options.risk: Hundreds of paginated requests per run on an unpublished unauthenticated rate limit.

items.recommendation: A as the default, with all three visible and sortable
items.why: It is the only measure that is stable between refreshes and cannot be inflated by a single trade. Showing all three costs nothing and removes the ambiguity from the reader's path.

items.title: Publish a calibration table before publishing any 'strategy'
items.problem: There is no demo portfolio, so no recommendation can be backed by executed trades. What the data can support is whether price bands resolve as their prices imply.

options.label: Calibration only, with sample sizes
options.detail: For each 10-cent price band, show n, mean implied probability and realised YES rate. Recommend nothing until n is large enough in the band of interest.
options.risk: Small n makes the table look more conclusive than it is if a reader ignores the counts.

options.label: Calibration plus a written strategy per topic
options.detail: Add prose strategies derived from the calibration bands.
options.risk: Turns an observation into advice on demo data that Kalshi itself says may not reflect real markets.

items.why: It keeps the site honest. Strategies belong on top of a portfolio with real fills (S1), where P&L can contradict them.

items.title: Verify and optionally add WebSocket streaming for the price chart
items.problem: Seconds-level history cannot come from candlesticks (1-minute minimum) and polling costs a request per tick. The docs recommend the WebSocket for current state, but streaming from a Pages origin is unverified.

options.label: Keep polling, label it clearly
options.detail: Current behaviour: poll one market every 15 s, keep second-level points in the browser, and label every point as polled rather than streamed.
options.risk: A quiet market looks flat between ticks.

options.label: Add an opt-in WebSocket toggle
options.detail: Connect to wss://external-api-ws.demo.kalshi.co/trade-api/ws/v2 on demand, subscribe to ticker and orderbook_delta, and merge into the chart.
options.risk: Unverified from the Pages origin; connection limits are undocumented for anonymous clients.

items.recommendation: A now, B after a browser test
items.why: Do not ship an unverified connection path. The chart already separates polled points from candlestick points so a reader knows what they are looking at.

items.title: Split 'read-only public data' from 'account data' at the architecture level
items.problem: One static site is currently asked to do both a public market dashboard and a private account dashboard. That mixing is what makes the key-handling question reappear.

options.label: Two surfaces
options.detail: This public site stays read-only market data. A separate private tool (Actions or backend) owns credentials and performance.
options.risk: Two places to check.

options.label: One site with a login
options.detail: Add authentication to the site so account pages are gated.
options.risk: GitHub Pages cannot authenticate users; this forces a backend anyway and adds a login surface to protect.

items.why: It removes a whole class of security questions from the public site instead of answering them carefully.

items.title: Add per-row data lineage to every table
items.problem: A reviewer should not have to trust the collector. They should be able to click through to the exact API response.

options.label: Link each row to its response URL
options.detail: Already implemented: every row links to the market endpoint and the list query that produced it.
options.risk: A response changes over time, so the link proves provenance, not the historical value.

options.label: Also archive the raw response
options.detail: Commit the compressed raw JSON per run so the exact bytes behind each row are preserved.
options.risk: Repository growth; needs a retention policy.

items.why: Links prove where a number came from; an archive proves what it was. The cost is a small daily artefact with a short retention.

items.title: Show liquidity, not just price, beside every ranking
items.problem: A market can rank first by notional while having one contract available at the touch, so a reader who tries to act on the ranking would move the price.

options.label: Add best-bid size columns
options.detail: yes_bid_size_fp and yes_ask_size_fp are already in the market object; surface them next to the price in every table.
options.risk: Sizes are stale by up to a cache interval.

options.label: Add a depth summary per market
options.detail: Pull depth=20 for the top markets and show total contracts within 5 cents of the touch.
options.risk: More requests per run.

items.recommendation: A plus B for the top 10 per topic
items.why: Best-bid size is nearly free and answers the question a reader actually has; depth summarises the rest without doubling the request count.

items.title: Audit scope completeness automatically
items.problem: The five topic queries are a construction, not a proof that every in-scope contract was found.

options.label: Diff all series against the scope queries
options.detail: Pull /series across all 19 categories each run and list any series that looks in-scope by title but was not matched by a scope query.
options.risk: A longer run and a review queue that needs a human.

options.label: Leave scope as documented
options.detail: State the query for each topic and accept that completeness is bounded by it.
options.risk: A genuinely in-scope market can be missed silently.

items.recommendation: A, as a nightly audit rather than every 15 minutes
items.why: Completeness is exactly the kind of claim that should be measured rather than asserted, but it does not need to run on the live cadence.

items.title: Surface the historical cutoffs and archive resolved markets
items.problem: Settled markets move to /historical/markets after a cutoff, so a resolution can vanish from the live endpoint the dashboard reads.

options.label: Store every resolved row seen
options.detail: The collector already appends resolved rows it observes; extend that to a durable per-topic archive keyed by ticker and result.
options.risk: Storage growth.

options.label: Read /historical/cutoff and query both tiers
options.detail: Display the three cutoff timestamps and query the historical endpoint for anything older.
options.risk: More requests and more code paths.

items.recommendation: A now, B when the first market is archived
items.why: The archive makes resolutions durable with almost no extra requests; the cutoff display becomes necessary only once a market actually crosses it.

items.title: Add a confidence band to every number, not just a source link
items.problem: A source link says where a value came from; it does not say how much that value can be trusted.

options.label: Three-state trust badge
options.detail: Verified (copied from an API response in this run), Stale (from an earlier run), Unverified (could not be confirmed) — applied to every cell.
options.risk: More visual noise.

options.label: Keep the current blank/flag convention
options.detail: Blank means the API returned nothing; flags live on one page.
options.risk: A reader has to know the convention.

items.recommendation: A for the tables that drive decisions
items.why: It makes the verification work visible at the point of use instead of one click away.
